claim: Drosophila larvae achieve robust odor gradient ascents through an alternation of approximately straight runs and turning events.
source: The Drosophila larva has the smallest known olfactory system analogous to that of vertebrates (Cobb, 1999; Bargmann, 2006b; Gerber and Stocker, 2007; Vosshall and Stocker, 2007). The larva achieves robust odor gradient ascents through an alternation of approximately straight runs and turning events (Gomez-Marin et al., 2011; Gershow et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citations to published work (Gomez-Marin et al., 2011; Gershow et al., 2012)

claim: The duration of runs is modulated by the sensory input: runs up the gradient are elongated while runs away from it are shortened.
source: The duration of runs is modulated by the sensory input: runs up the gradient are elongated while runs away from it are shortened (Gomez-Marin et al., 2011; Gershow et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citations to published work (Gomez-Marin et al., 2011; Gershow et al., 2012)

claim: Turns are preceded by stereotyped decreases in odor concentration.
source: It is known that turns are preceded by stereotyped decreases in odor concentration (Gomez-Marin et al., 2011; Gomez-Marin and Louis, 2012)
evidence: Supported by citations to published work (Gomez-Marin et al., 2011; Gomez-Marin and Louis, 2012)

claim: Animals with an olfactory system genetically reduced to a single functional OSN are still capable of robust chemotaxis.
source: Nonetheless, animals with an olfactory system genetically reduced to a single functional OSN are still capable of robust chemotaxis (Fishilevich et al., 2005; Louis et al., 2008)
evidence: Supported by citations to published work (Fishilevich et al., 2005; Louis et al., 2008)

claim: OSNs can act as differentiators that transiently normalize stimulus intensity.
source: We find that OSNs can act as differentiators that transiently normalize stimulus intensity—a property potentially derived from a combination of integral feedback and feed-forward regulation of olfactory transduction.
evidence: Supported by experimental data and modeling presented in the manuscript

claim: High activity levels of the OSN suppress turning, whereas low activity levels facilitate turning.
source: In olfactory virtual reality experiments, we report that high activity levels of the OSN suppress turning, whereas low activity levels facilitate turning.
evidence: Supported by experimental data from virtual reality experiments described in the manuscript

claim: The Or42a OSN firing rate displayed a clear amplification of changes in stimulus intensity.
source: Although the OSN activity appeared to follow the envelope of the stimulus time course, a closer examination revealed greater complexity in the neural response. The OSN firing rate displayed a clear amplification of changes in stimulus intensity, as illustrated by the activity associated with the replay of two consecutive runs, R1 and R2 (Figure 2F).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2F

claim: During the rising phase of the ramp, the neural activity increased in proportion with the derivative of the odor concentration.
source: During the rising phase of the ramp, the neural activity increased in proportion with the derivative of the odor concentration (Figure 3A).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3A

claim: During the falling phase of the ramp, the firing rate appeared to be driven by the stimulus intensity rather than the stimulus derivative.
source: During the falling phase of the ramp, the firing rate appeared to be driven by the stimulus intensity rather than the stimulus derivative (Figure 3B), suggesting that the response properties of the OSN differed for positive and negative gradients.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3B

claim: The OSN spiking activity peaked with the first derivative and not the absolute intensity of the stimulus during a sigmoid ramp.
source: To further test the hypothesis that the OSN encodes features related to the slope of the stimulus, we examined a sigmoid ramp (Figure 3C, right panel) for which the first derivative of the stimulus reached its maximum (gray arrow) prior to the stimulus intensity (magenta arrow). Consistent with the slope-sensitivity hypothesis, the OSN spiking activity peaked with the first derivative and not the absolute intensity of the stimulus.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3C

claim: A linear system-identification approach was insufficient to account for the firing patterns elicited by naturalistic stimuli.
source: We attempted to model the input–output relationship of the OSN by following a linear system-identification approach (Chichilnisky, 2001). To this end, we applied an M-sequence (pseudorandom binary sequence with nearly flat frequency spectrum) and reverse-correlation (Geffen et al., 2009), but discovered that the resulting linear filter was insufficient to account for the firing patterns elicited by naturalistic stimuli ('Materials and methods').
evidence: Supported by experimental data and modeling described in Materials and methods

claim: The composite IFF+IFB model led to a remarkably good fit between the output of the ODE model and the experimentally measured spiking activity.
source: The parameter set derived from the 10 odor ramps and naturalistic stimulus (Table 1) led to a remarkably good fit between the output of the ODE model and the experimentally measured spiking activity (experimental peristimulus time histogram PSTH—black line, results of the IFF+IFB model—blue line; Figure 4C,E,F, Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by experimental data and modeling results shown in Figure 4C,E,F and Figure 4—figure supplement 1

claim: The IFB pathway has a non-negligible impact on the dynamics of the OSN.
source: The contribution of the IFB motif to the dynamics of variable u is approximately 30% that of the IFF (cyan vs magenta curves, Figure 4D). This led us to conclude that the IFF pathway dominates the control of OSN spiking activity. The IFB pathway has nonetheless a non-negligible impact on the dynamics.
evidence: Supported by modeling results shown in Figure 4D

claim: The IFB motif does not contribute to the light-evoked response dynamics of the OSN.
source: Using the full set of linear and nonlinear light ramps together with a naturalistic pattern of light stimulation (Figure 6B), optimization of the parameters of the ODE system showed that the IFB pathway does not contribute to the light-evoked response dynamics of the OSN, suggesting that the integral feedback motif is specific to the odor-evoked activity (Table 1).
evidence: Supported by modeling results and parameter optimization described in Table 1

claim: Stationary levels of OSN firing rate lead to probabilistic transitions from run to turn.
source: The successful application of the stimulus-to-behavior GLM led us to conclude that: (1) stationary levels of OSN firing rate lead to probabilistic transitions from run to turn. When the OSN spiking activity remains constant, the probability of turning at a given time is largely independent of the duration of the run
evidence: Supported by experimental data and modeling results from the GLM

claim: The integrated neural-to-behavior model built on controlled conditions of stimulation (open-loop paradigm) was sufficient to predict run-to-turn transitions arising from free behavior in a virtual odor gradient (closed-loop paradigm).
source: The significance of the improvement in the predictive power of the test model relative to the controls was established by comparing the log-likelihood computed over the entire set of runs (Figures 6F, bottom panel and 'Materials and methods'). This allowed us to conclude that the integrated neural-to-behavior model built on controlled conditions of stimulation (open-loop paradigm) was sufficient to predict run-to-turn transitions arising from free behavior in a virtual odor gradient (closed-loop paradigm).
evidence: Supported by experimental data and statistical analysis shown in Figure 6F

claim: Larvae avoided the well region in the well landscape.
source: The IFF model correctly reproduced the strong inhibitory phase experimentally observed in the OSN spiking activity (Figure 7Bi, bottom panel). This inhibition was expected to generate a nearly deterministic release of turns. Consistently, larvae avoided the well region (Figure 7Bii).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7Bii

claim: The stimulus-to-behavior GLM predicted a modest increase in turn probability upon crossing of the rim without significant avoidance of the central area of the mesa.
source: The stimulus-to-behavior GLM predicted a modest increase in turn probability upon crossing of the rim without significant avoidance of the central area of the mesa (Figure 7E and Video 4). This prediction was corroborated by our experimental results (Figure 7Cii, bottom panel).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7Cii and predictions from the GLM shown in Figure 7E

claim: The average latency to turn was shortest for the well landscape (0.93 s) followed by the volcano (3.48 s).
source: As shown in Figure 7F, we found that the average latency to turn was shortest for the well landscape (0.93 s) followed by the volcano (3.48 s).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7F

claim: Significantly longer turn latencies were observed for the mesa and linear hat with no difference between the two conditions (6.6 s and 6.7 s, respectively).
source: We observed significantly longer turn latencies for the mesa and linear hat with no difference between the two conditions (6.6 s and 6.7 s, respectively).
evidence: Supported by experimental data and statistical analysis

claim: The test model predicted that runs were on average associated with a monotonic increase in the turn probability during several seconds before a turn in an odor gradient.
source: The model predicted that runs were on average associated with a monotonic increase in the turn probability during several seconds before a turn (Figure 8C).
evidence: Supported by modeling predictions shown in Figure 8C

claim: The likelihood of the ensemble of runs observed in the odor gradient was significantly larger than that computed for two control models.
source: Based on these predictions, we computed the likelihood of the ensemble of runs observed in the odor gradient. This likelihood was significantly larger than that computed for two control models (Figure 8D).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis shown in Figure 8D

claim: Individual OSNs of C. elegans and cockroaches function as bipolar detectors that selectively respond to either increases or decreases in stimulus intensity.
source: Most primary sensory neurons operate differently from proportional counters (Rieke, 1997; Song et al., 2012). Individual OSNs of C. elegans and cockroaches function as bipolar detectors that selectively respond to either increases or decreases in stimulus intensity (Tichy et al., 2005; Chalasani et al., 2007).
evidence: Supported by citations to published work (Rieke, 1997; Song et al., 2012; Tichy et al., 2005; Chalasani et al., 2007)

claim: A single larval OSN is sensitive to both the stimulus intensity and its first derivative.
source: In contrast with these binary sensory responses, we discovered that a single larval OSN is sensitive to both the stimulus intensity and its first derivative.
evidence: Supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript

claim: The enhanced information-processing capacity of primary olfactory neurons in the larva is consistent with the response characteristics of OSNs in adult flies, which encode complex dynamical features of airborne odorant stimuli.
source: The enhanced information-processing capacity of primary olfactory neurons in the larva is consistent with the response characteristics of OSNs in adult flies, which encode complex dynamical features of airborne odorant stimuli (Kim et al., 2011; Martelli et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citations to published work (Kim et al., 2011; Martelli et al., 2013)

claim: IFB motifs constitute the core mechanism of chemoreception in bacteria, olfactory transduction, and phototransduction.
source: IFB motifs constitute the core mechanism of chemoreception in bacteria, olfactory transduction, and phototransduction (Yi et al., 2000; De Palo et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citations to published work (Yi et al., 2000; De Palo et al., 2013)

claim: In adult flies, Nagel and Wilson (2011) investigated how the potential involvement of negative feedback on the olfactory transduction cascade could account for dynamical and adaptive features of OSN response.
source: In adult flies, Nagel and Wilson (2011) investigated how the potential involvement of negative feedback on the olfactory transduction cascade could account for dynamical and adaptive features of OSN response.
evidence: Supported by citation to published work (Nagel and Wilson, 2011)

claim: IFF motifs are implicated in the regulation of numerous cellular and developmental processes.
source: On the other hand, IFF motifs are implicated in the regulation of numerous cellular and developmental processes (Goentoro and Kirschner, 2009; Lim et al., 2013), and their contribution to sensory processing has been documented in recent work (Kato et al., 2014; Liu et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citations to published work (Goentoro and Kirschner, 2009; Lim et al., 2013; Kato et al., 2014; Liu et al., 2015)

claim: The OSN spiking activity follows a standard hyperbolic dose-response when stimulated by prolonged pulses of odor.
source: Our biophysical model of the olfactory transduction cascade shows that the spiking activity of the OSN follows a standard hyperbolic dose-response when stimulated by prolonged pulses of odor ('Materials and methods').
evidence: Supported by modeling results and experimental data described in Materials and methods

claim: The maximum OSN firing rate observed for IAA is modest.
source: In this regime, the maximum OSN firing rate we observed for IAA is modest (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1

claim: Changes in odor concentration occurring on a timescale relevant to the behavior—a second or shorter—can produce significantly higher (or lower) firing rates.
source: Changes in odor concentration occurring on a timescale relevant to the behavior—a second or shorter—can produce significantly higher (or lower) firing rates.
evidence: Supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript

claim: A single Or42a OSN combines the function of a slope (ON) detector in response to positive gradients and an OFF detector in response to negative gradients.
source: Our model indicates that a single Or42a OSN combines the function of a slope (ON) detector in response to positive gradients and an OFF detector in response to negative gradients.
evidence: Supported by modeling results and experimental data

claim: When larvae ascend Gaussian odor gradients originating from single odor sources, we expect high OSN firing rates.
source: When larvae ascend Gaussian odor gradients originating from single odor sources, we thus expect high OSN firing rates.
evidence: Inferred from the model and experimental results

claim: Robust inhibition of OSN spiking activity would result from motion that takes larvae down the odor gradient.
source: Robust inhibition of OSN spiking activity would result from motion that takes larvae down the odor gradient.
evidence: Inferred from the model and experimental results

claim: Under the conditions of open-loop light stimulation, OFF responses (offset inhibition of the OSN firing) promote turning, whereas ON responses (sustained high firing) suppress turning.
source: Under the conditions of open-loop light stimulation, we found that OFF responses (offset inhibition of the OSN firing) promote turning, whereas ON responses (sustained high firing) suppress turning (Figure 5).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5

claim: The accuracy of the model's output showed a striking dependence on the nonlinear transformation achieved by the olfactory transduction cascade.
source: The accuracy of the model's output showed a striking dependence on the nonlinear transformation achieved by the olfactory transduction cascade (Figure 5—figure supplement 3).
evidence: Supported by modeling results shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 3

claim: The information transmitted by a single larval OSN is sufficient to represent positive and negative odor gradients through the excitation and inhibition of spiking activity.
source: The information transmitted by a single larval OSN is sufficient to represent positive and negative odor gradients through the excitation and inhibition of spiking activity.
evidence: Supported by experimental data and modeling results

claim: Unlike for chemotaxis and thermotaxis in C. elegans where the ON and OFF pathways are associated with different cellular substrates, the same larval OSN is capable of controlling up-gradient and down-gradient sensorimotor programs.
source: Unlike for chemotaxis and thermotaxis in C. elegans where the ON and OFF pathways are associated with different cellular substrates (Chalasani et al., 2007; Suzuki et al., 2008), the same larval OSN is capable of controlling up-gradient and down-gradient sensorimotor programs.
evidence: Supported by experimental data and citations to published work (Chalasani et al., 2007; Suzuki et al., 2008)

claim: This observation echoes findings recently made for thermotaxis in the Drosophila larva.
source: This observation echoes findings recently made for thermotaxis in the Drosophila larva (Klein et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citation to published work (Klein et al., 2015)

claim: It corroborates the idea that sensory representations are rapidly transformed into motor representations in the circuit controlling chemotaxis.
source: Furthermore, it corroborates the idea that sensory representations are rapidly transformed into motor representations in the circuit controlling chemotaxis (Luo et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citation to published work (Luo et al., 2014)

claim: The network of interneurons located in the larval antennal lobe is expected to participate in the processing of olfactory information arising from the OSNs.
source: In addition, the network of interneurons located in the larval antennal lobe (Das et al., 2013) is expected to participate in the processing of olfactory information arising from the OSNs (Asahina et al., 2009; Larkin et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by citations to published work (Das et al., 2013; Asahina et al., 2009; Larkin et al., 2010)

claim: Adult-fly PNs encode the second derivative of olfactory stimuli.
source: As adult-fly PNs encode the second derivative of olfactory stimuli (Kim et al., 2015) including circuit elements downstream of the OSNs in the present multilevel model are expected to improve the accuracy of the behavioral predictions of the model.
evidence: Supported by citation to published work (Kim et al., 2015)

claim: Exposure to an odor produces gradient ascent even in larvae with a genetically manipulated olfactory system reduced to a single OSN.
source: Odors are generally attractive to Drosophila larvae (Cobb, 1999). Exposure to an odor produces gradient ascent even in larvae with a genetically manipulated olfactory system reduced to a single OSN (Fishilevich et al., 2005; Louis et al., 2008).
evidence: Supported by citations to published work (Cobb, 1999; Fishilevich et al., 2005; Louis et al., 2008)

claim: Or42a is an odorant receptor with a well-characterized tuning profile that includes the odorant isoamyl acetate (IAA).
source: We examined the behavior of larvae with a single functional OSN expressing Or42a, an odorant receptor with a well-characterized tuning profile that includes the odorant isoamyl acetate (IAA) (Fishilevich et al., 2005; Kreher et al., 2008; Asahina et al., 2009).
evidence: Supported by citations to published work (Fishilevich et al., 2005; Kreher et al., 2008; Asahina et al., 2009)

claim: For large odor droplets, diffusion from the source creates a radially symmetric gradient that can be approximated by a stationary Gaussian distribution.
source: For large odor droplets, diffusion from the source creates a radially symmetric gradient that can be approximated by a stationary Gaussian distribution (Louis et al., 2008).
evidence: Supported by citation to published work (Louis et al., 2008)

claim: For smaller odor droplets such as those used in the present study, the temporal evolution of the odor gradient cannot be neglected.
source: For smaller odor droplets such as those used in the present study, the temporal evolution of the odor gradient cannot be neglected.
evidence: Supported by experimental observations and modeling

claim: On average, larvae terminate their runs when motion is directed down the gradient where the odor concentration is decreasing.
source: On average, larvae terminate their runs when motion is directed down the gradient where the odor concentration is decreasing (Gomez-Marin et al., 2011; Gershow et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citations to published work (Gomez-Marin et al., 2011; Gershow et al., 2012)

claim: Turns are suppressed when the direction of motion is along the gradient and the odor concentration is increasing.
source: In contrast, turns are suppressed when the direction of motion is along the gradient and the odor concentration is increasing.
evidence: Supported by experimental observations

claim: Recordings from the 3-min stimulation led to consistent patterns of neural activity in different preparations.
source: Recordings from this 3-min stimulation led to consistent patterns of neural activity in different preparations (Figure 2D).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2D

claim: OSN activity peaked several seconds before the stimulus intensity during run R2.
source: Run R2 brought the larva close to and then beyond the peak of the gradient. When stimulated by the corresponding time course of the odor concentration, OSN activity peaked several seconds before the stimulus intensity (Figure 2F, arrows).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2F

claim: Minute fluctuations in odor concentration were strongly amplified in the OSN spiking dynamics.
source: Minute fluctuations in odor concentration were strongly amplified in the OSN spiking dynamics (bursts marked by a sharp # symbol in Figure 2F).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2F

claim: The temporal profile of the light ramps was identical to the odor ramps.
source: The response properties of the OSN were then studied for a family of stimulus ramps induced by light instead of odor. The temporal profiles of the light ramps were identical to the odor ramps
evidence: Supported by experimental design

claim: The temporal pattern of the OSN activity elicited by the light ramps was comparable to that elicited by the odor ramps.
source: In this regime, the temporal pattern of the OSN activity elicited by the light ramps was comparable to that elicited by the odor ramps (experimental PSTH—black lines, Figure 4E,F and Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4E,F and Figure 4—figure supplement 1

claim: This close similarity in the input–output relationships permitted us to substitute the odor stimulus with light.
source: This close similarity in the input–output relationships permitted us to substitute the odor stimulus with light.
evidence: Supported by experimental data showing comparable responses

claim: The goodness of fit of the pure IFF motif, when applied to both light and odor stimulations, was comparable.
source: Notably, the goodness of fit of the pure IFF motif, when applied to both light and odor stimulations, was comparable (Table 2).
evidence: Supported by quantitative analysis shown in Table 2

claim: The nonlinear-dynamical response properties of the OSN stimulated by odor and light ramps can be well approximated by the IFF motif.
source: In conclusion, the nonlinear-dynamical response properties of the OSN stimulated by odor and light ramps can be well approximated by the IFF motif, even though the IFB motif brings a non-negligible contribution to the modeling of odor-evoked response dynamics.
evidence: Supported by modeling results and experimental data

claim: The integration-differentiation scaling function S(x, t) plays a role similar to the 'input gain control' resulting from lateral inhibition of the local interneuron on the projection neurons in the adult antennal lobe.
source: The integration-differentiation scaling function S(x, t) plays a role similar to the 'input gain control' resulting from lateral inhibition of the local interneuron on the projection neurons in the adult antennal lobe (Olsen et al., 2010) with the notable difference that the rescaling takes place within the primary OSN and that it is driven by the temporal integration of changes in the stimulus intensity.
evidence: Supported by mathematical analysis and citation to published work (Olsen et al., 2010)

claim: This operation appears related to the adaptive rescaling of the spike dynamics observed in adult-fly OSNs.
source: This operation appears related to the adaptive rescaling of the spike dynamics observed in adult-fly OSNs (Kim et al., 2011; Nagel and Wilson, 2011).
evidence: Supported by citations to published work (Kim et al., 2011; Nagel and Wilson, 2011)

claim: The most salient features encoded in the activity pattern of the Or42a>ChR2 OSN are: (1) rapid increases in firing rate triggered by abrupt positive changes in the stimulus intensity (accelerations); (2) a relaxation of the firing rate toward stationary activity when the first derivative of the stimulus is null or constant (no acceleration or deceleration); (3) decreases in firing rate in response to stimulus decelerations.
source: By examining the analytical solution of the IFF motif under the quasi-steady-state approximation (Equation 1), we discovered that the most salient features encoded in the activity pattern of the Or42a>ChR2 OSN are: (1) rapid increases in firing rate triggered by abrupt positive changes in the stimulus intensity (accelerations); (2) a relaxation of the firing rate toward stationary activity when the first derivative of the stimulus is null or constant (no acceleration or deceleration); (3) decreases in firing rate in response to stimulus decelerations.
evidence: Derived from mathematical analysis of the model

claim: The spiking activity of the neuron is strongly inhibited upon abrupt return to the stimulus baseline.
source: In addition, we experimentally observed that (4) the spiking activity of the neuron is strongly inhibited upon abrupt return to the stimulus baseline.
evidence: Supported by experimental observations

claim: Sustained spiking activity of the OSN would suppress turning while inhibition of the OSN would facilitate turning.
source: We asked whether these features bore any relevance to the control of run-to-turn transitions during odor gradient ascent. We hypothesized that sustained spiking activity of the OSN would suppress turning while inhibition of the OSN would facilitate turning.
evidence: Hypothesis based on experimental observations

claim: Experiments were conducted on blind larvae to avoid innate photophobic behavior.
source: To avoid innate photophobic behavior (Sawin-McCormack et al., 1995; Kane et al., 2013), experiments were conducted on blind larvae ('Materials and methods').
evidence: Supported by experimental design and citations to published work (Sawin-McCormack et al., 1995; Kane et al., 2013)

claim: When an exponential ramp was played to the larva, the pattern of light stimulation was executed as long as the larva remained in a run state.
source: When an exponential ramp was played to the larva, the pattern of light stimulation was executed as long as the larva remained in a run state. Upon interruption of the run, the light intensity was reset to baseline.
evidence: Supported by experimental design

claim: The motion of the larva had no influence on the stimulation pattern it experienced in the open-loop experimental protocol.
source: As the motion of the larva had no influence on the stimulation pattern it experienced, this experimental protocol featured a sensorimotor loop that is essentially 'open'.
evidence: Supported by experimental design

claim: When the behavior was modulated by changes in light intensity, the majority of the runs associated with an exponential ramp did not terminate before the falling phase of the ramp.
source: When the behavior was modulated by changes in light intensity, the majority of the runs associated with an exponential ramp did not terminate before the falling phase of the ramp.
evidence: Supported by experimental observations

claim: Upon constant light stimulation, the instantaneous turn probability was largely independent of the duration of the ongoing run.
source: Upon constant light stimulation, we found that the instantaneous turn probability was largely independent of the duration of the ongoing run (light gray line, Figure 5C).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5C

claim: The turn probability was strongly modulated by the exponential light ramp.
source: In contrast, the turn probability was strongly modulated by the exponential light ramp (black line, Figure 5C).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5C

claim: During the rising phase of the ramp (0–8 s), turning was suppressed below the value corresponding to basal stimulation.
source: During the rising phase of the ramp (0–8 s), turning was suppressed below the value corresponding to basal stimulation.
evidence: Supported by experimental data

claim: A sharp increase in turn probability was observed during the falling phase of the ramp.
source: Conversely, a sharp increase in turn probability was observed during the falling phase of the ramp.
evidence: Supported by experimental data

claim: The modulation of the turn probability by the light-evoked spiking activity corroborated the idea that strong activation of the OSN efficiently suppresses turning, whereas inhibition promotes turning.
source: The modulation of the turn probability by the light-evoked spiking activity corroborated the idea that strong activation of the OSN efficiently suppresses turning, whereas inhibition promotes turning.
evidence: Supported by experimental data

claim: The probability of turning remained approximately constant when the OSN activity was stationary.
source: As the probability of turning remained approximately constant when the OSN activity was stationary, we hypothesized that the relationship between the OSN spiking activity and the control of run-to-turn transitions could be captured by a simple model where the time-varying probability of turning was described by the combination of a constant term (λ0) and a term proportional to the current OSN firing rate: λ0+ λ1y(t).
evidence: Supported by experimental observations

claim: The stimulus-to-behavior GLM accurately reproduces the time courses of the experimental turn probability for the linear and nonlinear ramps.
source: For the linear and nonlinear ramps, the stimulus-to-behavior GLM accurately reproduces the time courses of the experimental turn probability (blue lines, Figures 5E,F).
evidence: Supported by modeling results shown in Figures 5E,F

claim: The goodness of fit of the GLM was clearly contingent on the nonlinear transformation achieved by the OSN.
source: The goodness of fit of the GLM was clearly contingent on the nonlinear transformation achieved by the OSN (Table 4).
evidence: Supported by quantitative analysis shown in Table 4

claim: The OSN activity is sensitive to the slope of the ramp.
source: Consistent with our finding that the OSN activity is sensitive to the slope of the ramp, we found that the performance of the control GLM was improved by combining the light intensity (x) with its first derivative (dx/dt) (Figure 5—figure supplement 3).
evidence: Supported by experimental data and modeling results shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 3

claim: For the majority of ramps, the improvement of the control GLM with the first derivative did not match the quality of the fit produced by the integrated stimulus-to-behavior GLM.
source: For the majority of ramps, this improvement did, however, not match the quality of the fit produced by the integrated stimulus-to-behavior GLM (Table 4).
evidence: Supported by quantitative analysis shown in Table 4

claim: The nonlinear response characteristics of the OSN have a noticeable influence on the control of orientation behavior.
source: We concluded that the nonlinear response characteristics of the OSN have a noticeable influence on the control of orientation behavior.
evidence: Supported by experimental data and modeling results

claim: The larva ascended the light gradient and remained in the vicinity of its peak by implementing a series of runs and directed turns.
source: Figure 6A illustrates the behavior of an Or42a>ChR2 larva in a light gradient. As observed for the odor-evoked behavior (Gomez-Marin et al., 2011), the larva ascended the light gradient and remained in the vicinity of its peak by implementing a series of runs and directed turns.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6A and citation to published work (Gomez-Marin et al., 2011)

claim: The spiking activity of the OSN displayed considerable processing of the stimulation pattern.
source: In Figure 6B, we examined how the Or42a>ChR2 OSN responds to a replay of the light intensity changes experienced during the trajectory shown in Figure 6A. The spiking activity of the OSN displayed considerable processing of the stimulation pattern.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6B

claim: This transformation of the stimulus was well captured by the IFF model.
source: This transformation of the stimulus was well captured by the IFF model.
evidence: Supported by modeling results

claim: The initiation of a turn was typically preceded by a steady increase in the predicted probability of turning.
source: Correlating the predictions of the model with the termination of the actual runs revealed that the initiation of a turn was typically preceded by a steady increase in the predicted probability of turning (Figure 6B,C and Video 1).
evidence: Supported by experimental data and modeling predictions shown in Figure 6B,C

claim: The stimulus-to-behavior GLM predicted that the stimulus downslope was transformed into a monotonic increase in turn probability.
source: As reported in previous work (Gomez-Marin et al., 2011), we found that the stimulus intensity decreases steadily for several seconds prior to a turn (data not shown). Accordingly, the stimulus-to-behavior GLM predicted that the stimulus downslope was transformed into a monotonic increase in turn probability (light blue line, Figure 6E).
evidence: Supported by modeling predictions shown in Figure 6E and citation to published work (Gomez-Marin et al., 2011)

claim: Neither control displayed a substantial increase in turn probability prior to turning.
source: In contrast to the test GLM, neither control displayed a substantial increase in turn probability prior to turning (red and back dashed lines, Figure 6E).
evidence: Supported by modeling results shown in Figure 6E

claim: The integrated neural-to-behavior model built on controlled conditions of stimulation (open-loop paradigm) was sufficient to predict run-to-turn transitions arising from free behavior in a virtual odor gradient (closed-loop paradigm).
source: This allowed us to conclude that the integrated neural-to-behavior model built on controlled conditions of stimulation (open-loop paradigm) was sufficient to predict run-to-turn transitions arising from free behavior in a virtual odor gradient (closed-loop paradigm).
evidence: Supported by experimental data and statistical analysis

claim: The tendency of larvae to initiate turning upon crossing of the volcano's rim was evident from the set of runs that moved from the outer to the inner edge of the volcano.
source: We therefore expected to observe turn suppression during the rising phase of the ramp and turn facilitation during the falling phase of the ramp. The tendency of larvae to initiate turning upon crossing of the volcano's rim was evident from the set of runs that moved from the outer to the inner edge of the volcano (Figure 7Aii, bottom panel).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7Aii

claim: The alternation between turn suppression and turn facilitation resulted in a zigzagging of trajectories across the rim of the volcano.
source: The alternation between turn suppression and turn facilitation resulted in a zigzagging of trajectories across the rim of the volcano.
evidence: Supported by experimental observations

claim: The integrated stimulus-to-behavior GLM predicted a rise in the turn probability prior to the interruption of a run in the volcano landscape.
source: The integrated stimulus-to-behavior GLM predicted a rise in the turn probability prior to the interruption of a run (Figure 7E and Video 2).
evidence: Supported by modeling predictions shown in Figure 7E

claim: The GLM predicted a dramatic increase in turn probability following the crossing of the rim in the well landscape.
source: Consistently, larvae avoided the well region (Figure 7Bii). Such a behavior was correctly described by the GLM, which predicted a dramatic increase in turn probability following the crossing of the rim (Figure 7E and Video 3).
evidence: Supported by modeling predictions shown in Figure 7E and experimental data shown in Figure 7Bii

claim: The OSN underwent a mild drop in spiking activity before a stationary value was reached during the transition from an exponential rise in light intensity to a plateau value in the mesa landscape.
source: During the transition from an exponential rise in light intensity to a plateau value, the OSN underwent a mild drop in spiking activity before a stationary value was reached—a feature accurately reproduced by the IFF motif (Figure 7Ci).
evidence: Supported by experimental data and modeling results shown in Figure 7Ci

claim: The stimulus-to-behavior GLM predicted no significant difference between the behavior evoked by the mesa and the linear hat landscapes.
source: The IFF model faithfully reproduced this counterintuitive observation. At a behavioral level, the stimulus-to-behavior GLM predicted no significant difference between the behavior evoked by the mesa and the linear hat landscapes (Figure 7E and Video 5).
evidence: Supported by modeling predictions shown in Figure 7E

claim: These predictions were in good agreement with the free behavior of larvae in the linear hat landscape.
source: These predictions were in good agreement with the free behavior of larvae (Figure 7Dii, bottom panel).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7Dii

claim: The use of synthetic light landscapes permitted us to experimentally demonstrate that sustained OSN spiking activity suppresses turning during free behavior, whereas inhibition of the OSN activity promotes run-to-turn transitions in a nearly deterministic manner.
source: In conclusion, the use of synthetic light landscapes permitted us to experimentally demonstrate that sustained OSN spiking activity suppresses turning during free behavior, whereas inhibition of the OSN activity promotes run-to-turn transitions in a nearly deterministic manner.
evidence: Supported by experimental data from synthetic light landscapes

claim: The relatively simple linear control underlying the GLM trained on the behavior of larvae experiencing stereotyped open-loop light stimulations is sufficient to account for the control of behavior elicited under conditions of closed-loop light stimulation.
source: This approach established that the relatively simple linear control underlying the GLM trained on the behavior of larvae experiencing stereotyped open-loop light stimulations is sufficient to account for the control of behavior elicited under conditions of closed-loop light stimulation.
evidence: Supported by experimental data and modeling results

claim: In a real odor landscape, larvae accumulated at the peak of the gradient with a dispersal notably larger than that observed in a light gradient.
source: In a real odor landscape (Figure 8A), larvae accumulated at the peak of the gradient with a dispersal notably larger than that observed in a light gradient (Figure 6D).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 8A and Figure 6D

claim: This apparent decrease in orientation performances can be partly explained by the shallower geometry of the odor gradient.
source: This apparent decrease in orientation performances can be partly explained by the shallower geometry of the odor gradient (Figure 8—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by analysis shown in Figure 8—figure supplement 1

claim: The structure and parameters of the integrated stimulus-to-behavior GLM form a solid conceptual basis to describe how the sensory dynamics of single OSNs influence run-to-turn transitions during naturalistic behavior.
source: Together, these results establish that the structure and parameters of the integrated stimulus-to-behavior GLM form a solid conceptual basis to describe how the sensory dynamics of single OSNs influence run-to-turn transitions during naturalistic behavior (Video 6).
evidence: Supported by experimental data and modeling results

claim: A similar specialization into ON-OFF detection pathways has been observed for thermotaxis in C. elegans and motion perception in adult flies.
source: A similar specialization into ON-OFF detection pathways has been observed for thermotaxis in C. elegans (Suzuki et al., 2008) and motion perception in adult flies (Joesch et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by citations to published work (Suzuki et al., 2008; Joesch et al., 2010)

claim: Combining the IFF and IFB motifs was necessary to recapitulate the richness of OSN dynamics elicited by naturalistic olfactory stimuli.
source: Using a parameter optimization approach, we found that a pure IFF motif is sufficient to approximate the response properties of the OSN. Combining the IFF and IFB motifs was nonetheless necessary to recapitulate the richness of OSN dynamics elicited by naturalistic olfactory stimuli (Figure 4 and Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by modeling results shown in Figure 4 and Figure 4—figure supplement 1

claim: Consistent with the model proposed by Nagel and Wilson (2011), our numerical simulations indicate that the integral feedback applies to the signaling pathway specific to the odorant receptor (OR).
source: Consistent with the model proposed by Nagel and Wilson (2011), our numerical simulations indicate that the integral feedback applies to the signaling pathway specific to the odorant receptor (OR).
evidence: Supported by modeling results and citation to published work (Nagel and Wilson, 2011)

claim: Nagel and Wilson have suggested that a diffusible effector—potentially intracellular calcium—inhibits the activity of the OR, thereby affecting the onset and offset kinetics of the OSN response.
source: Nagel and Wilson have suggested that a diffusible effector—potentially intracellular calcium—inhibits the activity of the OR, thereby affecting the onset and offset kinetics of the OSN response.
evidence: Supported by citation to published work

claim: The IFF motif would describe a regulatory mechanism acting on components of the transduction pathway downstream from the OR.
source: By contrast, the IFF motif would describe a regulatory mechanism acting on components of the transduction pathway downstream from the OR (Gu et al., 2009).
evidence: Supported by citation to published work (Gu et al., 2009)

claim: It is plausible that the IFF regulation is also mediated by intracellular calcium.
source: It is plausible that the IFF regulation is also mediated by intracellular calcium.
evidence: Speculative statement based on knowledge of the field

claim: Positive derivatives in stimulus intensity excite the OSN.
source: Upon changes in odor concentration, the dose–response function describing the OSN spiking activity is transiently rescaled (or 'normalized') by the short-term history of the stimulus derivative ('memory' on characteristic time scale of 1 s, see 'Materials and methods'). As a result, positive derivatives in stimulus intensity excite the OSN.
evidence: Supported by mathematical analysis and experimental data

claim: Negative derivatives can inhibit the OSN firing rate in a manner consistent with the stimulus-offset inhibitions observed in adult-fly OSNs.
source: Negative derivatives can inhibit the OSN firing rate in a manner consistent with the stimulus-offset inhibitions observed in adult-fly OSNs (Hallem et al., 2004; Nagel and Wilson, 2011).
evidence: Supported by mathematical analysis and citations to published work (Hallem et al., 2004; Nagel and Wilson, 2011)

claim: We applied a GLM to describe the link between the OSN spiking dynamics and the probability of switching from a run to a turn.
source: We applied a GLM to describe the link between the OSN spiking dynamics and the probability of switching from a run to a turn (Figure 5D).
evidence: Supported by modeling approach described in Figure 5D

claim: We combined the biophysical model for the OSN spiking dynamics with the GLM to make robust predictions about closed-loop behavior in virtual and in real odor gradients.
source: Ultimately, we combined the biophysical model for the OSN spiking dynamics with the GLM to make robust predictions about closed-loop behavior in virtual and in real odor gradients (Figures 6–8).
evidence: Supported by modeling results and experimental data shown in Figures 6–8

claim: It will be important to define whether the sensorimotor principles proposed for the Or42a OSN can be generalized to OSNs expressing other odorant receptors.
source: In the future, it will be important to define whether the sensorimotor principles proposed for the Or42a OSN can be generalized to OSNs expressing other odorant receptors (Fishilevich et al., 2005; Kreher et al., 2008; Mathew et al., 2013).
evidence: Speculative statement about future research directions with citations to published work (Fishilevich et al., 2005; Kreher et al., 2008; Mathew et al., 2013)

claim: The network of interneurons located in the larval antennal lobe is expected to participate in the processing of olfactory information arising from the OSNs.
source: In addition, the network of interneurons located in the larval antennal lobe (Das et al., 2013) is expected to participate in the processing of olfactory information arising from the OSNs (Asahina et al., 2009; Larkin et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by citations to published work (Das et al., 2013; Asahina et al., 2009; Larkin et al., 2010)

claim: Our work suggests that the computations achieved by the antennal lobe are not strictly necessary to guide robust chemotaxis.
source: Although our work suggests that the computations achieved by the antennal lobe are not strictly necessary to guide robust chemotaxis (see also 'Materials and methods'), the function of the transformation carried out by the synapse between the Or42a OSN and its cognate projection neuron (PN) remains to be elucidated in the larva (Ramaekers et al., 2005; Asahina et al., 2009; Masuda-Nakagawa et al., 2009).
evidence: Supported by experimental results and citations to published work (Ramaekers et al., 2005; Asahina et al., 2009; Masuda-Nakagawa et al., 2009)

claim: Including circuit elements downstream of the OSNs in the present multilevel model are expected to improve the accuracy of the behavioral predictions of the model.
source: As adult-fly PNs encode the second derivative of olfactory stimuli (Kim et al., 2015) including circuit elements downstream of the OSNs in the present multilevel model are expected to improve the accuracy of the behavioral predictions of the model.
evidence: Speculative statement based on citation to published work (Kim et al., 2015)

claim: It will be interesting to examine the validity of the present model for the sensorimotor control of other aspects of larval chemotaxis such as turn orientation through lateral head casts (casting-to-turn transitions).
source: It will be interesting to examine the validity of the present model for the sensorimotor control of other aspects of larval chemotaxis such as turn orientation through lateral head casts (casting-to-turn transitions).
evidence: Speculative statement about future research directions

claim: In adult flies, turn orientation is determined by the crossing of the boundaries of odor plumes: upon encountering of an odor plume, flies veer upwind whereas exiting the plume initiates lateral and vertical casting.
source: In adult flies, turn orientation is determined by the crossing of the boundaries of odor plumes: upon encountering of an odor plume, flies veer upwind whereas exiting the plume initiates lateral and vertical casting (van Breugel and Dickinson, 2014)—an orientation strategy related to the surge-and-cast response of moths (Carde and Willis, 2008).
evidence: Supported by citations to published work (van Breugel and Dickinson, 2014; Carde and Willis, 2008)

claim: To orient in a rapidly changing olfactory landscape, the OSNs of various flying insects are capable of tracking rapid odor pulses on sub-second timescales and differentiating these signals.
source: To orient in a rapidly changing olfactory landscape, the OSNs of various flying insects are capable of tracking rapid odor pulses on sub-second timescales and differentiating these signals (Kim et al., 2011; Fujiwara et al., 2014; Szyszka et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citations to published work (Kim et al., 2011; Fujiwara et al., 2014; Szyszka et al., 2014)

claim: Whether the processing of turbulent olfactory inputs involves more temporal integration than that described by the sensorimotor model proposed here remains to be elucidated.
source: Whether the processing of turbulent olfactory inputs involves more temporal integration than that described by the sensorimotor model proposed here remains to be elucidated.
evidence: Speculative statement about future research

claim: The Drosophila larva offers a unique opportunity to delineate the neural circuit basis of behavior.
source: Finally, the Drosophila larva offers a unique opportunity to delineate the neural circuit basis of behavior (Ohyama et al., 2013, 2015).
evidence: Supported by citations to published work (Ohyama et al., 2013, 2015)

claim: Interdisciplinary approaches combining behavioral screens, functional imaging, and circuit reconstruction on the one hand, and computational modeling and robotics on the other hand, should improve our understanding of how brains with reduced numerical complexity exploit streams of sensory information to direct action selection.
source: Interdisciplinary approaches combining behavioral screens, functional imaging, and circuit reconstruction on the one hand (Yao et al., 2012), and computational modeling and robotics on the other hand (Grasso et al., 2000; Webb, 2002; Izquierdo and Lockery, 2010; Ando et al., 2013), should improve our understanding of how brains with reduced numerical complexity exploit streams of sensory information to direct action selection.
evidence: Speculative statement about future research directions with citations to published work (Yao et al., 2012; Grasso et al., 2000; Webb, 2002; Izquierdo and Lockery, 2010; Ando et al., 2013)
